usedCounterFrames: deep-work-ch01 | The paradox is that a day can look full while the best mind never touches demanding work. The sharper test is whether attention went to depth or to shallow tasks that merely prove availability.

deep-work-ch02 | The paradox is that focus can look like a comfort preference while acting like an economic advantage: intact attention helps you learn hard things faster and produce work that is harder to copy.
deep-work-ch03 | Most people assume rare work disappears because it stopped mattering. Often it disappears because the workplace rewards signals that are easier to see than serious thought.

deep-work-ch04 | The paradox is that meaning often comes less from the size of the task than from the quality of attention: a real challenge, a clear standard, and enough absorption to care about the result.

deep-work-ch05 | Most people think deep work happens when they feel disciplined. It happens more reliably when the calendar, place, rules, and shutdown routine make concentration the default next action.
deep-work-ch06 | The paradox is that boredom looks like wasted time while quietly training focus: the mind learns, in ordinary restless moments, whether every urge gets rewarded immediately.
deep-work-ch07 | The paradox is that a tool can be genuinely useful and still be a bad trade. A stronger standard asks whether it substantially supports a valued goal after attention cost is counted.
deep-work-ch08 | The paradox is that shallow work becomes controllable only after you give it more explicit attention: estimate it, batch it, tighten it, and its real cost becomes visible.

deep-work-ch09 | The paradox is that a deep life is not built from dramatic bursts of focus when stakes get high. It is built from repeated structures, defended standards, and attention choices that survive ordinary weeks.
usedTryThisNowFrames: deep-work-ch01 | Open yesterday's calendar and mark one block D for demanding work and one block S for shallow support. Circle the hour that got your clearest mind.
deep-work-ch02 | Choose one skill or project where quality matters. Give it thirty silent minutes today, then write one sentence about what improved when the task had continuity.
deep-work-ch03 | Look at one team norm today. Identify whether it rewards visible responsiveness or concentrated progress, then write one replacement signal that would prove real output.
deep-work-ch04 | Pick one task you normally rush. For ninety seconds, name the standard that would make it done well, then give the next ten minutes to that standard only.
deep-work-ch05 | Before the next demanding task, write four details: where you will sit, how long you will work, what is allowed, and what finished means.
deep-work-ch06 | The next time you wait in line or ride an elevator, keep the phone away for sixty seconds. Notice the urge, name it once, and let it pass without feeding it.
deep-work-ch07 | Choose one optional digital tool. Write the important goal it serves, the cost it imposes, and whether a thirty-day removal would damage what matters.
deep-work-ch08 | Open tomorrow's calendar and give shallow work a named window. Put one demanding task outside that window, with a start time and output written beside it.
deep-work-ch09 | Choose one deep-work structure you will keep for the next seven days: a morning block, a tool rule, a shutdown ritual, or a shallow-work budget. Put it on the calendar now.
